english.html: Who, arrived from Spain, having a wooden leg, as a year before had been set down by the soldier (of whom mention has been made above), presents a petition narrating the whole imposture, asking to be heard. The Court orders that he shall be heard, holding him under close arrest [l'arrest clos: confinement to an assigned place] in the keeping of the guard of the palace.

This word Arrest, in our French tongue, is taken in two ways. The first, for a final judgment and decree of a sovereign court; and so many think that it is drawn from the Greek ἄρεστον, which is as much as to say an ordinance of a magistrate. Whence it seems also, says that great Budé, that we err in writing and pronouncing it with a double R, seeing that ἄρεστον, from which it is drawn, is written only with a single R a. The second, for a kind of imprisonment, proceeding from the command and injunction of the magistrate made to some person not to stir from a certain place which he assigns to him b: as in our context.

notes.citation: Guillaume Budé (Guil. Budée), Annotationes in Pandectas, on the last law of Digest 1.9 (De senatoribus; l. fin. = D. 1.9.12, Ulpian), at its end
notes.original: Guil. Budée en la Loy fin. ſur la fin. D. de ſenator.
notes.gloss: Budé's Annotationes (1508) are arranged as a commentary on the Digest; the passage deriving arrest from ἀρεστόν stands under this law. Locus not verified against the printed Annotationes.

notes.citation: Digest 43.29 (De homine libero exhibendo), l. 2 (D. 43.29.2, Venuleius; the title has four laws, and the second is taken as printed); Digest 35.1 (De condicionibus et demonstrationibus et causis et modis eorum quae in testamento scribuntur), the law containing the paragraph beginning Titio centum (the law's incipit is not printed; fragment not identified)
notes.original: l. ij. D. de lib. exhib. l. P. Tirio centũ. D. de con. & demon.
notes.gloss: The print's P. is its sort for the paragraph sign §, and Tirio a wrong sort for Titio. Cited for the Roman sense of being kept or detained in a place without being in a prison: the interdict for producing a free man wrongfully held, and a legacy conditioned on the legatee's not leaving a place.

english.html: Nevertheless, that he shall be confronted with the said du Tilh, prisoner, with Pierre Guerre, Bertrande de Rols and the sisters of the said Martin, together with certain other witnesses who were the principal of those who had so pertinaciously assured that the prisoner was truly Martin Guerre. He is heard; he sets down and gives tokens upon the same interrogations

'l. ij. D. de li. ho. exhib.' — the title De libero homine exhibendo (D. 43.29), which the book cites as 'D. de lib. ho. exhib.' at annot-084 n. g and annot-086 n. f and 'D. de liber. exhib.' at annot-020 n. h; a bare 'de lib. exhib.' would be the neighbouring title De liberis exhibendis. Moderate confidence: decided from the parallel citations, not from the glyphs.; The title is *De libero homine exhibendo* (D. 43.29), the interdict for producing a detained free man, which is the point of Coras's second sense of *arrest*; annot-086's margin prints the same title as *D. de lib. ho. exhib.*, so the *ho* of reading B is expected and reading A drops it.
